meta.description: Not the Buddha. It’s the French proverb ‘Tout comprendre, c’est tout pardonner,’ made famous by Tolstoy’s War and Peace and misattributed to Buddha by 1910.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'To understand everything is to forgive everything'?
meta.ogDescription: Not the Buddha. A French proverb voiced in Tolstoy’s War and Peace (1869), pinned on Gautama Buddha only in the 20th century.

answer.label: Not the Buddha — an old French proverb
answer.authorName: An anonymous French proverb (‘Tout comprendre, c’est tout pardonner’)
answer.authorDates: Traditional French maxim · current in 19th-century French & Russian letters · no single author
answer.sourceLine: There is no Buddhist text behind this line. It is the French proverb “Tout comprendre, c’est tout pardonner” — famously voiced by Princess Mary in Tolstoy’s War and Peace (1869), whose translators render it “To understand all is to forgive all.” It was pinned on Gautama Buddha, without any source, only in the 20th century.

source.excerpt: “Tout comprendre, c’est tout pardonner.” — Princess Mary, urging her brother Prince Andrew toward compassion for his wife’s weaknesses. The English editions footnote the line: “To understand all is to forgive all.”
trail: Fake Buddha Quotes traces the saying to the French proverb and Madame de Staël, not the Buddha ↗.
Wikiquote files it under Buddha’s Misattributed section — a French proverb first tied to Buddha in Farm Journal (1910) ↗.
The proverb is documented in Tolstoy’s War and Peace (1869), spoken by Princess Mary ↗.
source.excerptNote: The popular English wording — “To understand everything is to forgive everything” — is a loose translation of this same French proverb, not a phrase from any Buddhist text.

sourceLink.text: War and Peace, Book 1, Chapter 28 on Wikisource

source.rightsNote: The saying is an anonymous French proverb (“Tout comprendre, c’est tout pardonner”) with no single identifiable author, and the exact English wording is not tied to one specific pre-1931 translation. Tolstoy’s War and Peace (1869) is itself public domain, but the free-floating English proverb has no fixed rights status, so we assert none.

author.name: Leo Tolstoy
author.heading: The line’s most famous home
author.metaLine: 1828–1910 · Russian novelist · War and Peace & Anna Karenina
author.bio: Leo Tolstoy did not coin this saying — he put the ready-made French proverb “Tout comprendre, c’est tout pardonner” into the mouth of Princess Mary in War and Peace (1869), where she uses it to urge compassion. That novel is the earliest widely-read source where an English-reading audience met the exact sentiment. The proverb itself is folk wisdom of the French salons, not Tolstoy’s invention — and certainly not the Buddha’s.

misattribution.heading: Who it’s wrongly pinned on
misattribution.intro: A tidy maxim about compassion is a magnet for prestige names. This one has drifted across several.

items.why: There is no Buddhist scripture behind it. Wikiquote places it in Buddha’s Misattributed section, noting it “seems to have first become attributed to Gautama Buddha without citation of sources” in Farm Journal Vol. 34 (1910) ↗.
Frequently credited, but Fake Buddha Quotes finds no hard evidence she wrote the maxim ↗; her novel Corinne (1807) carries a related but different line about understanding making one indulgent.
Tolstoy voiced the proverb through Princess Mary in War and Peace (1869) ↗, but he was quoting a known French saying, not coining it.

misattribution.truthLine: It is an anonymous French proverb — “Tout comprendre, c’est tout pardonner” — wrongly attached to the Buddha only in the early 20th century ↗.

context.heading: Why the line travels so well
lead: The proverb compresses a real philosophical claim — that complete understanding of why a person acts dissolves the grounds for blame — into six balanced words. That symmetry is exactly what makes it quotable, and exactly what makes it easy to re-home under whichever wise name a poster prefers.

Attaching it to the Buddha lends the maxim an air of ancient, cross-cultural authority it never earned. In fact its documented life is thoroughly European and modern: a French salon proverb, quoted by a Russian novelist, then floated free on the 20th-century internet.
context.pull: Understand fully, and there is nothing left to forgive — a French salon idea, not a Buddhist one.
